title: Seed pages and their owners

story: The brain needs about 35 pages before agents can lean on it, and the people who know the answers do not have weeks to write them. So Claude Code drafts them: for each page it reads the code and documents the page should be based on, and writes a short page. In one afternoon there are 18 engineering drafts, and they read well.

One of them, about how a code run reaches the on-prem client (the part of our product that runs inside a customer's network), says in its first step that the cloud opens a gRPC connection to each client. It sounds reasonable. It is the opposite of the truth: the client opens the connection, because customer networks accept no connections from outside. A backend engineer would see the mistake in a second. Nova, planning a change to that code, would build on it.
hook.question: How do we use AI to write the first pages quickly without turning the brain into a place where confident mistakes live?

read.h: Start from the questions people ask
p: The first question is not "what do we know?" but "what do people keep asking?". A page nobody looks for costs an owner a review every quarter and helps nobody. So the first pages, the seed pages, come from real demand: questions in public engineering channels over the last six months, the gaps the last two new hires ran into, and the topics our backend skills explain most often. The aim is about 18 engineering pages, 6 product pages, 6 decision records and 5 runbooks, and cross-team topics come first (cloud and client, CI, the QA environments, releases), because that is where one person's knowledge blocks everyone else.

Each seed page gets an owner before anyone writes a word. The owner is a person or a guild team that agreed, in Slack, to check the page and keep it current. Each page also lists two to five sources the draft must be built from. All of this goes into one file, the seed plan, which is deleted once the pages exist. Notice what is not on the list: how to write code in fcp. That is what the codebase skills teach. Brain pages explain how the system works and why.

code.text:
pages:
  - path: engineering/code-run-path.md
    title: How a code run reaches the on-prem client
    owner: "@RhinoHealth/backend-guild"
    sources:
      - https://github.com/RhinoHealth/fcp/tree/main/common/fcp_common/rhinoAgentRpc
      - https://github.com/RhinoHealth/fcp/tree/main/client/rhinoOnPrem/rhinoAgentRpc/handlers
    demand: "<link to the public thread where someone asked this>"
  - path: runbooks/integration-test-lock.md
    title: What to do when integration tests wait for the QA lock
    owner: "@RhinoHealth/devops"
    sources:
      - https://github.com/RhinoHealth/fcp/blob/main/.github/workflows/_cloud-int-tests-reusable-aws.yml
    demand: "onboarding gap: both new hires asked in their first week"
  # ... about 33 more, each owner asked on Slack before drafting starts

notes.text: An owner who already said yes. A page without a willing owner is not started.
The sources are the draft's only input. A fact that is not in them does not belong on the page.
Why the page exists: a real question, or a gap a new hire hit. These questions are reused later to test the brain.

p: The drafting is the part AI is good at. For each entry in the seed plan, the author runs Claude Code in an fcp checkout with the brain repo added (claude --add-dir ../rnd-kb), gives it the page's sources and the page template, and asks for a short page with five parts: a one-paragraph summary, the path step by step, why it is built this way, what breaks if you change it, and where to look first. Pages stay one or two screens long and link to code by path instead of pasting it.

Every draft is saved with confidence: low. That one word tells every reader, and later the Slack bot, that no person has checked this page yet. Before opening a pull request, the author reads the draft against its sources once, and follows one strict rule: a claim with no source is deleted, not softened. Writing "usually" or "probably" in front of a guess does not make it true; it only makes it harder to spot.

title: How a code run reaches the on-prem client
owner: "@RhinoHealth/backend-guild"
reviewed: 2026-10-20
review_every: 90d
confidence: low # AI draft from the sources below; the owner raises it after checking
sources:

# How a code run reaches the on-prem client

**In short.** The client runs inside the customer's network and opens the connection
to the cloud; the cloud never connects in. Work travels back over that stream.

## Step by step
1. <each step names the file that does it, checked against the sources>

## Why it is built this way
Customer networks don't accept inbound connections, and patient data stays there.

## What breaks if you change it
The protos are a contract with clients already installed at customers.

## Where to look first
`client/rhinoOnPrem/rhinoAgentRpc/handlers/`, `cloud/rhinoCloud/rhinoAgentRpc/`

notes.text: low: an AI draft. Search, the index and the bot all show this, so nobody mistakes it for a checked page.
Each step names the file that does it, so the owner can check it in one click.
The part readers need most and code shows least: what you must not break.

p: Drafts go to their owners as pull requests in rnd-kb, one pull request per owner with only that owner's few pages, and the owner is the reviewer, not the person who drafted them. A reviewer who has three of their own pages to read actually reads them; a reviewer handed thirty skims.

The owner reads each claim next to its source. Wrong claims get fixed, and claims the owner cannot confirm get deleted. Then the owner sets the confidence honestly and sets reviewed to the day of the check. high means "I checked this against main this week". med means "mostly right, but I did not check one part". The diff below is the whole change on the client page once its owner had checked it: two lines of frontmatter, plus a Jira ticket the owner added as a source. Raising confidence is a promise with a name and a date on it, which is why only the owner makes it.

notes.text: reviewed moves to the day the owner actually checked the page.
high: the owner checked every claim against main.
Owners often add the source they know best, such as the ticket that changed this code.

read.h: When the brain is ready for agents
p: Drafts are useful to people who know to treat them as leads, but agents need checked pages. So the plan sets a bar: at least 30 pages at med or high, counted with effective confidence, so a page that is more than twice overdue does not count however confident its file says it is. When kb lint on main shows 30 such pages, Nova and Byte (our review agent) start reading the brain through the kb skill, the seed plan is deleted, and the index is shared in a public channel.

Owners also find gaps while they review: "this page should mention the QA lock". Each gap becomes a line in an existing page or a short new page with its own owner, never one big page that nobody can review in one sitting.

deeper.h: Go deeper: decision records and runbooks
p: Two kinds of seed pages have a fixed shape. A decision record, or ADR (architecture decision record), lives in decisions/ as ADR-NNNN-<slug>.md and has four parts: a status (proposed, accepted or superseded), the context that was true when we decided, the decision in plain words with its numbers, and the consequences, good and bad. The first ones record the brain's own home and this quarter's agent-platform choices, such as one fresh VM per run. An ADR answers "why is it like this?", which code can never answer.

A runbook is for the moment something is red: integration tests waiting for the QA lock, main is red, Byte failed on my PR, FCP Lab will not start. Every step in a runbook is a command or a link, because the reader is stressed and needs to act, not to read.

lab.title: Review an AI draft as its owner
needs: A terminal and a text editor
lab.goal: Check two AI-drafted pages claim by claim against a small stand-in for fcp, fix or delete each claim, and raise their confidence only when every claim holds.

guess.q: An AI draft has four numbered claims. Three match the code. For the fourth, "a failed message is retried five times", you can find nothing in the sources or the code. What do you do with it?

options.text: Keep it, but write "usually" in front of it
options.why: A softened guess is still a guess, and now it is harder to spot. Readers, and agents, will still act on it.

options.text: Keep it and set the page to med instead of high
options.why: med means one part is unchecked, not that a guess may stay. The claim would still be read as a fact.

options.text: Delete the claim, then raise the page once the remaining claims are checked
options.why: A claim nobody can source does not belong on the page. If the retry count matters, someone finds the real answer and adds it with a source.

2. Runs for different components or clouds do not wait for each other.

follow.say: Add a small script that counts how many pages count as checked, using effective confidence like every brain tool does.
follow.do:
cat > progress.py <<'EOF'
import sys
from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

DAYS = {"30d": 30, "90d": 90, "180d": 180, "365d": 365}
GOAL = 30


def effective(meta: dict, today: date) -> str:
    age = (today - meta["reviewed"]).days
    return "low" if age > 2 * DAYS[meta.get("review_every", "90d")] else meta["confidence"]


today = date.today()
checked = 0
for path in sorted(Path(sys.argv[1]).rglob("*.md")):
    meta = yaml.safe_load(path.read_text().split("---")[1])
    confidence = effective(meta, today)
    checked += confidence in ("high", "med")
    print(f"{confidence:<4}  reviewed {meta['reviewed']}  {path}")
print(f"checked pages (med or high): {checked} of the {GOAL} we need")
EOF
uv run --with pyyaml python progress.py kb

solution.text:
---
title: Integration tests wait for the QA lock
owner: "@RhinoHealth/devops"
reviewed: <today>
review_every: 90d
confidence: high # checked against the workflow by the owner
sources:
  - https://github.com/RhinoHealth/fcp/blob/main/.github/workflows/_cloud-int-tests-reusable-aws.yml
---
# Integration tests wait for the QA lock

1. There is one lock per component per cloud (the concurrency group qa-lock-<component>-<cloud>),
   so only one run of the same component on the same cloud uses the QA environment at a time.
2. Runs for different components or clouds do not wait for each other.

lab.fix: Before a weekly update, a teammate wanted a better number and made progress.py "simpler": sed 's/confidence = effective(meta, today)/confidence = meta["confidence"]/' progress.py > progress-simple.py. Run uv run --with pyyaml python progress-simple.py kb: the count goes up by one, and nobody reviewed anything. Find which page it now counts, and explain why that page must not count as checked.
explain: Why does every AI draft start at confidence: low, even when it looks right?
Why is a claim with no source deleted instead of softened with "usually"?
Why does the page owner review the pull request, and not the person who drafted the pages?
lab.done: Both drafts are checked, every remaining claim has a place in the code that supports it, and progress.py counts 3 checked pages.

check.q: An owner reviewing a draft finds a claim they cannot confirm in the code or in any source. What should they do?

options.why: A claim nobody can source is a guess. Removing it costs a sentence; leaving it can mislead every agent that reads the page.

options.text: Keep it with "probably" in front of it
options.why: Softening makes a guess sound careful, but readers still act on it, and it becomes harder to find later.

options.text: Keep it and lower the page to med
options.why: med means one part was not checked. It does not make room for a claim that has no source at all.

check.q: When may a page's confidence be raised to high?

options.why: Lint checks the frontmatter and the links, never whether the body is true.

options.text: When the AI draft cites a source for every claim
options.why: A cited source is where to check, not proof that the claim matches it. The client draft cited the right folder and still had step 1 backwards.

options.text: When the page's owner has checked every claim against main, and sets reviewed to that day
options.why: high is a promise with a name and a date on it. Only the owner can make it, and the reviewed date says when.

check.q: Why are the seed pages chosen from questions people really asked, instead of covering every part of the system?

options.text: Because Claude Code can only draft 35 pages
options.why: It could draft hundreds in a day. The limit is people: every page needs an owner who checks it every quarter.

options.text: Because a small set of pages people use can stay checked, and the questions later test whether the brain answers them
options.why: Each page costs its owner a review every few months, so it must earn its place. The same real questions later become the test set for the brain.

options.text: Because kb lint fails on more than 35 pages
options.why: Lint has no page limit. The bar of 30 checked pages is a minimum for agents, not a maximum.

p: Shai owns the seeding. He commits rnd-kb/seed-plan.yml with about 18 engineering, 6 product, 6 decision and 5 runbook entries, each with an owner from OWNERS.yml who accepted in Slack, two to five sources, and the demand that justifies it. He drafts the engineering pages with Claude Code (claude --add-dir ../rnd-kb in an fcp checkout), then the product pages from Drive "Rhino Team/Product" and Jira epics, the decision records starting with ADR-0001 (brain home) and the agent-platform ADRs (one fresh VM per run, Temporal orchestrates, the broker and gateway hold the keys, TypeScript on Node 24), and four runbooks. Every draft sets owner, reviewed, review_every 90d, confidence low, sources and applies_to, passes kb lint and kb index, and goes out as one PR per owner.

The guilds then review: at least 15 of the 18 engineering pages at med or high by the end of week 6, and at least 30 owned pages at med or high overall. When kb lint on main shows 30, seed-plan.yml is deleted and index.md is shared in a public engineering channel; that is the bar for Nova and Byte to read the brain through the kb skill, and BRAIN-QA uses these checked pages as its sources.

tickets.why: The seed plan: 35 pages from real demand, each with an owner who agreed and its sources.
The 18 engineering drafts at confidence: low, one PR per owner.
The product pages, the first decision records and the runbooks, drafted the same way.
Owners check the engineering pages and raise confidence only after checking against the code.
Owners check the second batch, gap pages get written, and the 30-page bar is reached.

words.plain: The first 35 or so brain pages, chosen from questions people really asked.
The person or team that agreed to check a page against the code and keep it current.
A page written by Claude Code from listed sources, saved at confidence: low until its owner checks it.
One YAML file listing each seed page with its owner, sources and the demand behind it; deleted when the pages exist.
A page that records one decision: its status, the context, the decision and its consequences.

review.q: Explain the difference between high and med in one sentence each.
review.a: high: the owner checked every claim against main recently. med: mostly right, but the owner did not check one part.

review.q: A draft cites the right folder but gets the direction of a connection backwards. Which step of the process should catch it, and how?
review.a: The owner's review: reading each claim next to its source, for example finding which side creates the gRPC channel. Lint cannot catch it, because the frontmatter is valid.

review.q: Why does the 30-page bar count effective confidence and not the confidence written in the file?
review.a: A page more than twice overdue may no longer be true, whatever its file says. Counting it would let old pages make the brain look ready for agents.

remember: AI writes the first draft at confidence: low; only the page's owner, after checking every claim against its source and deleting what cannot be checked, raises it.
